106946.q: Which profession did Albrecht von Haller study for at university?
106946.e: Haller studied medicine and graduated as a doctor in Leiden in the Netherlands in 1727. He was also a poet and a botanist.
106946.m: Albrecht von Haller was a doctor.

106947.q: In which century did Albrecht von Haller live?
106947.e: Haller lived during the Enlightenment. He was one of the most versatile scholars of his age.
106947.m: Albrecht von Haller was a scholar of the Enlightenment.

106948.q: In 1760, Saussure offered a reward for the first ascent of which mountain?
106948.e: Saussure wanted to study the highest mountain in the Alps scientifically. The first ascent was only achieved in 1786 by Jacques Balmat and Michel-Gabriel Paccard.
106948.m: Saussure encouraged the first ascent of Mont Blanc.

106949.q: Which city did Horace-Bénédict de Saussure come from?
106949.e: Saussure taught philosophy and natural history at the academy of his home city. From there he made many journeys into the Alps.
106949.m: Saussure was a naturalist from Geneva.

106950.q: What did Saussure do when he stood on the summit of Mont Blanc?
a: He jumped off with a parachute
106950.e: On the summit Saussure measured air pressure and temperature. For him, research was what mattered most.
106950.m: Saussure even did research on Mont Blanc.

106951.q: Which instrument for measuring humidity did Saussure develop?
106951.e: A human hair gets longer in damp air and shorter in dry air. Saussure used this to measure humidity.
106951.m: A hair hygrometer measures humidity with a hair.

106952.q: What did Saussure measure with his cyanometer?
106952.e: The device consisted of a colour scale from white to dark blue. With it, Saussure compared how blue the sky was in different places.
106952.m: The cyanometer measures how blue the sky is.

106953.q: What did Saussure study on his journeys in the Alps?
106953.e: In a work of several volumes, Saussure described the rocks, glaciers, plants and weather of the Alps.
106953.m: Saussure studied the nature of the Alps.

106954.q: How did Switzerland once honour Horace-Bénédict de Saussure?
a: He was pictured on a banknote
A canton was named after him
Mont Blanc was named after him
106954.e: Saussure was pictured on the twenty-franc note of the sixth series. It was in circulation until 2000.
106954.m: Saussure was on a Swiss banknote.

106955.q: Saussure is often regarded as a co-founder of which activity?
106955.e: Saussure combined mountain climbing with scientific research. He made the high mountains a destination for travellers and researchers.
106955.m: Saussure is seen as one of the founders of mountaineering.

106956.q: What did Saussure build to capture the heat of the sun?
106956.e: In his solar box the temperature rose sharply under several panes of glass. It is seen as a forerunner of today’s solar collectors.
106956.m: Saussure built an early solar collector.

106957.q: Which theory about the Earth’s history made Louis Agassiz famous?
106957.e: Agassiz interpreted boulders and polished rock surfaces as traces of huge glaciers. He spread the idea that large parts of Europe were once covered in ice.
106957.m: Agassiz made the ice age theory well known.

106958.q: Which country did Agassiz emigrate to in 1846?
106958.e: Agassiz crossed the Atlantic to give lectures and stayed there. He became a professor at Harvard University.
106958.m: From 1846 Agassiz worked in the USA.

106959.q: Which group of animals did Agassiz study in his great work on fossils?
106959.e: In several volumes Agassiz described hundreds of fossil species. The work made him known throughout Europe while he was still young.

106960.q: At which Swiss academy was Agassiz a professor from 1832?
106960.e: Agassiz taught natural history at the academy in Neuchâtel. From there he carried out his glacier research.
106960.m: Agassiz was a professor in Neuchâtel.

106961.q: Where did Agassiz and his helpers stay while they were studying a glacier?
a: In a shelter under a boulder on the ice
In a grand hotel in Bern
On a boat on Lake Thun
106961.e: The simple shelter, the “Hôtel des Neuchâtelois”, was under a large boulder on the Unteraar Glacier. Agassiz and his team watched the glacier there for several summers.
106961.m: Agassiz did his research right on the glacier.

106962.q: Why is Louis Agassiz also strongly criticised today?
106962.e: Agassiz claimed that human groups were of different value. Such ideas are now regarded as scientifically wrong and inhumane.
106962.m: Agassiz was an important but also controversial scientist.

106963.q: In which canton was Louis Agassiz born in 1807?
106963.e: Agassiz was born in Môtier on Lake Murten, where his father was the pastor. Today the village belongs to the municipality of Mont-Vully.
106963.m: Agassiz came from Môtier in the canton of Fribourg.

106964.q: What did Agassiz measure on a glacier with the help of poles he drove into the ice?
106964.e: The poles moved down the valley with the ice. From how far they moved over time, the speed of flow could be calculated.
106964.m: Glaciers flow slowly down the valley.

106965.q: In which city was the physicist Auguste Piccard born in 1884?
106965.e: His father was a professor of chemistry at the university of his home city. Piccard then studied at ETH Zurich.

106966.q: What did Auguste Piccard reach in 1931 in a balloon, as one of the first people to do so?
a: The other side of the Atlantic
The whole way round the Earth
106966.e: Piccard wanted to study cosmic rays at high altitude. To do this, he rose far above the clouds and the weather.
106966.m: In 1931 Auguste Piccard flew into the stratosphere by balloon.

106967.q: Roughly what height did Piccard reach on his balloon flight in 1931?
106967.e: That was almost twice as high as Mount Everest. Without a special cabin, the balloonists would not have survived there.
106967.m: In 1931 Piccard rose to a height of almost 16 kilometres.

106968.q: What did Auguste Piccard want to study with his balloon flight into the stratosphere?
106968.e: Piccard wanted to measure cosmic rays, which come from space, at high altitude. To do this, he rose far above the clouds and the weather.
106968.m: In the stratosphere, Piccard studied radiation from space.

106969.q: What did Bertrand Piccard, Auguste Piccard’s grandson, achieve in 1999?
a: The first non-stop balloon flight around the world
The first landing on the Moon
The first ascent of Mount Everest
The first dive to the seabed
106969.e: In 1999 Bertrand Piccard and Brian Jones flew round the Earth in the balloon “Breitling Orbiter 3” without landing. The Piccard family is known for its records in the air and under water.
106969.m: In 1999 Bertrand Piccard flew round the world in a balloon.

106970.q: What was new about the gondola of Piccard’s stratosphere balloon?
a: It was an airtight pressurised cabin
106970.e: At high altitude the air is too thin to breathe. The sealed aluminium sphere kept enough air pressure inside.
106970.m: Piccard travelled in an airtight pressurised cabin.

106971.q: Which comic character by Hergé is said to have been inspired by Auguste Piccard?
106971.e: Hergé saw the tall, thin professor in Brussels. The absent-minded inventor in the Tintin comics has his features.
106971.m: Professor Calculus is modelled on Auguste Piccard.

106972.q: Auguste Piccard’s brother Jean was also a balloonist. How was he related to Auguste?
a: He was his brother, ten years older
106972.e: Jean Piccard was Auguste Piccard’s twin brother. He was a chemist, later lived in the USA and also flew into the stratosphere with his wife Jeannette.
106972.m: Auguste Piccard had a twin brother called Jean.

106973.q: At which university did Auguste Piccard become a professor of physics in 1922?
106973.e: Piccard taught for many years at the Free University in Belgium’s capital. From there he also prepared his balloon flights.
106973.m: Auguste Piccard was a professor in Brussels.

106974.q: What was Conrad Gessner’s great work “Historia animalium” about?
106974.e: The work described all the animals known at the time, with many woodcuts. It is seen as the beginning of modern zoology.
106974.m: Gessner wrote an enormous book about animals.

106975.q: In which city did Conrad Gessner live and work?
106975.e: Gessner was born there in 1516 and spent most of his life in the city. He taught at the Carolinum, the forerunner of the university.
106975.m: Conrad Gessner was a scholar from Zurich.

106976.q: Which mountain near Lucerne did Gessner climb and describe in 1555?
106976.e: At that time people believed that the ghost of Pontius Pilate haunted the mountain. Gessner climbed it anyway and raved about mountain walking.

106977.q: What did Conrad Gessner die of in 1565?
106977.e: As a doctor, Gessner cared for the sick during an epidemic and caught the disease himself. He was only 49 years old.

106978.q: Why is Gessner regarded as the father of bibliography?
a: He listed thousands of books and authors
106978.e: In his “Bibliotheca universalis” he listed the writings of around 3,000 authors. It was a first attempt to organise all known knowledge.
106978.m: Gessner made a huge list of books.

106979.q: Which writing tool did Gessner describe in 1565 as one of the first to do so?
106979.e: Gessner drew a stick of graphite held in a wooden holder. Quills, on the other hand, had been known for a long time.
106979.m: Gessner described a pencil as early as 1565.

106980.q: On the old Swiss banknote with Conrad Gessner, what could be seen next to his portrait?
a: Plants and animals from his books
106980.e: Gessner was pictured on the old fifty-franc note. It also showed plants and animals from his books.
106980.m: Gessner was pictured on the old fifty-franc note.

106981.q: Which flower did Gessner describe and draw in 1559 as one of the first in Europe?
106981.e: Gessner saw it in a garden in Augsburg. The flower originally came from Central Asia and reached Europe via the Ottoman Empire.
106981.m: Gessner described the tulip early on.

106982.q: Which office did Conrad Gessner hold in his home city?
106982.e: Gessner had studied medicine and looked after the health of the people. Besides that, he did research tirelessly.

106983.q: Which country did the clockmaker and mathematician Jost Bürgi come from?
106983.e: Jost Bürgi was born in 1552 in Lichtensteig in the Toggenburg. He taught himself a lot.

106984.q: What was Jost Bürgi’s original profession?
106984.e: Bürgi built extremely precise clocks and instruments. This skill made him sought after at royal courts.

106986.q: Where did Jost Bürgi work as a clockmaker?
106986.e: Bürgi first worked for the Landgrave in Kassel and later for the Emperor in Prague. Princes paid a lot for his precise clocks.
106986.m: Bürgi built clocks for princes and emperors.

106987.q: Why did astronomers in Bürgi’s time need particularly precise clocks?
a: To record when they observed a star
To make trains run on time
106987.e: To calculate the movements in the sky, you had to know exactly when each observation was made. Bürgi built clocks for this at the imperial court in Prague.

106988.q: Which famous astronomer did Bürgi work with in Prague?
106988.e: The astronomer used Bürgi’s calculation methods and instruments for his calculations. He thought very highly of Bürgi.
106988.m: Bürgi worked together with Johannes Kepler.

106989.q: Which new feature did Bürgi’s clocks have early on?
106989.e: Bürgi built some of the first clocks that ran so precisely that showing seconds was worthwhile. This was important for observing the stars.
106989.m: Bürgi built early clocks that showed seconds.

106990.q: What did Bürgi build to show the movement of the stars?
106990.e: His globes turned like the starry sky, driven by clockwork. Some of them are on display in museums today.
106990.m: Bürgi built elaborate celestial globes with clockwork.

106991.q: What was the proportional compass, which Jost Bürgi improved, used for?
106991.e: With the proportional compass you could easily enlarge or reduce distances in the same ratio. This helped when drawing maps and plans.
106991.m: The proportional compass helps with enlarging and reducing.

106992.q: What did Scheuchzer think he could see in the fossil “Homo diluvii testis”?
a: A human from the Great Flood
106992.e: The Latin name means “man, witness of the Flood”. Scheuchzer thought the skeleton was a drowned sinner.
106992.m: Scheuchzer thought a fossil was a human from the Great Flood.

106993.q: What is the fossil “Homo diluvii testis” really?
106993.e: The fossil comes from Öhningen on Lake Constance. Today the extinct species is called Andrias scheuchzeri.
106993.m: The “Flood man” was really a giant salamander.

106994.q: How did people find out that the “Flood man” was not a human?
a: The bones were compared with living animals
106994.e: In 1811 the scientist Georges Cuvier uncovered more bones and compared them with the skeletons of animals alive today. This showed that it was a giant salamander.
106994.m: Comparisons with living animals cleared up the mistake.

106995.q: Which country did the naturalist Johann Jakob Scheuchzer come from?
106995.e: Scheuchzer lived in Zurich from 1672 to 1733. He was a doctor and studied the nature of the Alps.

106996.q: Which mythical creatures did Scheuchzer collect reports about on his journeys in the Alps?
106996.e: Many mountain people told of seeing dragons. Scheuchzer wrote down the reports and sorted them by canton.
106996.m: Scheuchzer collected dragon stories from the Alps.

106997.q: What did Scheuchzer want to explain in a large illustrated work using the scientific knowledge of his time?
a: Fairy tales by the Brothers Grimm
106997.e: In his work “Physica sacra”, also called the Copper Bible, he explained events from the Bible with science. It contains hundreds of copper engravings.
106997.m: Scheuchzer combined the Bible with scientific knowledge.

106998.e: For a long time his map was the most accurate picture of the Swiss Confederation. It was often reprinted.
106998.m: Scheuchzer drew a map of Switzerland in 1712.

106999.q: With which instrument did Scheuchzer work out the height of mountains on his journeys?
106999.e: The higher you climb, the lower the air pressure gets. From the difference in pressure, the height could be estimated.
106999.m: You can work out heights with a barometer.

107000.q: Which large research institute in the canton of Aargau bears Paul Scherrer’s name?
107000.e: The Paul Scherrer Institute, PSI for short, is in Villigen and Würenlingen in Aargau. It is the largest research institute for natural sciences and engineering in Switzerland.
107000.m: The Paul Scherrer Institute is in Aargau.

107001.q: Which rays are used in the method for studying crystal powders that Scherrer helped to develop?
107001.e: The rays are diffracted by the powder and form typical rings on a film. From these you can read the structure of the crystals.
107001.m: You can study crystals with X-rays.

107002.q: What did Paul Scherrer study with X-rays?
107002.e: Together with Peter Debye, Scherrer developed a method in 1916 for working out the structure of crystal powders with X-rays.
107002.m: Paul Scherrer studied crystals with X-rays.

107003.q: At which university was Paul Scherrer a professor of physics for decades?
107003.e: From 1920 Scherrer headed the physics institute there. His lectures were so popular that many people who were not students came too.
107003.m: Paul Scherrer taught at ETH Zurich.

107004.q: Which country did the physicist Paul Scherrer come from?
107004.e: Paul Scherrer was born in St Gallen in 1890 and later taught at ETH Zurich.
107004.m: Paul Scherrer was a Swiss physicist.

107005.q: Scherrer helped to found which European research organisation near Geneva?
107005.e: The organisation was founded in 1954 and today runs the largest particle accelerators in the world. Scherrer campaigned for it to be based in Switzerland.
107005.m: Paul Scherrer helped to set up CERN.

107006.q: Which field of research did Scherrer particularly promote in Switzerland after the Second World War?
107006.e: Scherrer headed a federal commission for research into atomic energy. He wanted Switzerland to be able to keep up in this field.
107006.m: Paul Scherrer promoted nuclear research in Switzerland.

107007.q: Which term did Fritz Zwicky coin in 1933 for invisible mass in space?
107007.e: Zwicky called it “dunkle Materie” in German, meaning dark matter. What it is made of is still not known today.
107007.m: Fritz Zwicky introduced the term dark matter.

107008.q: What did Zwicky observe in a cluster of galaxies that pointed to missing mass?
a: The galaxies were moving far too fast
The galaxies were all the same size
107008.e: At such high speeds the cluster should have flown apart. So much more mass than you can see is needed to hold it together.
107008.m: Galaxies that move too fast give away invisible mass.

107009.q: Which term for a huge star explosion did Zwicky coin together with Walter Baade?
107009.e: Such an explosion can briefly shine brighter than a whole galaxy. With this term Zwicky and Baade distinguished it from ordinary novae.
107009.m: Zwicky and Baade coined the word supernova.

107011.q: In which country did the Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky do research for decades?
107011.e: From 1925 Zwicky worked at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena. He used telescopes in California to search for star explosions.
107011.m: Fritz Zwicky did his research in the USA.

107012.q: Roughly how many supernovae did Zwicky discover?
107012.e: For years Zwicky searched systematically with a telescope on Mount Palomar. Hardly anyone in his time found more of these star explosions.
107012.m: Fritz Zwicky discovered over a hundred supernovae.

107013.q: Which blood vessels are the finest in the human body?
107013.e: Capillaries, also called hair vessels, are the smallest blood vessels. They form a fine network that runs through almost all tissues.
107013.m: The capillaries are the finest blood vessels in the body.

107014.q: How thick is the wall of a capillary?
107014.e: The wall of a capillary is made of just one thin layer of endothelial cells. That is why substances can pass through it easily.
107014.m: Capillaries have a wafer-thin wall of just one layer of cells.

107015.q: What is the main job of the capillaries?
a: Exchanging substances between blood and tissue
107015.e: In the capillaries, oxygen and nutrients pass from the blood into the tissue. In return, the blood takes up carbon dioxide and waste.
107015.m: In the capillaries, blood and tissue exchange substances.

107016.q: Roughly what is the diameter of a typical capillary?
107016.e: Capillaries are only about 5 to 10 micrometres wide, which is much thinner than a hair. A micrometre is a thousandth of a millimetre.
107016.m: A capillary is much thinner than a human hair.

107017.q: How do red blood cells move through the narrowest capillaries?
a: Not at all, they stay still
107017.e: The narrowest capillaries are hardly wider than a red blood cell. The blood cells change shape and squeeze through one at a time.
107017.m: In narrow capillaries, red blood cells line up one by one.

107018.q: Between which blood vessels do the capillaries lie?
a: Between the windpipe and the lungs
Between the stomach and the intestines
107018.e: The blood flows from the arteries through the fine capillaries into the veins and from there back to the heart.
107018.m: The capillaries connect arteries and veins.

107019.q: Which gas do the capillaries in a working muscle mainly give off?
107019.e: The blood brings oxygen to the muscle cells, which need it to make energy. In return the blood takes up carbon dioxide.
107019.m: In muscles, the capillaries give oxygen to the cells.

107020.q: Where do capillaries in the lungs take up oxygen?
107020.e: The air sacs (alveoli) are surrounded by dense networks of capillaries. There, oxygen passes from the air you breathe into the blood.
107020.m: A network of capillaries surrounds the air sacs in the lungs.

107021.q: How fast does blood flow in the capillaries compared with the large arteries?
107021.e: All the capillaries together have a huge total cross-section, so the blood flows very slowly there. This leaves enough time for substances to be exchanged.
107021.m: Blood flows slowly in the capillaries so that the exchange can happen.

107022.q: What is the large artery in the groin that supplies the leg with blood called?
107022.e: The femoral artery, in Latin arteria femoralis, runs from the groin down the thigh. It is the main artery of the leg.
107022.m: The leg is mainly supplied by the femoral artery.

107023.q: Which artery is squeezed by the cuff when blood pressure is measured?
a: The brachial artery in the upper arm
107023.e: The cuff goes round the upper arm and squeezes the artery there. Its Latin name is arteria brachialis.
107023.m: When measuring blood pressure, the upper arm artery is briefly squeezed.

107024.q: Which artery runs along the little-finger side of the forearm?
107024.e: The forearm has two main arteries along its two bones. The ulna is on the little-finger side, and the ulnar artery runs next to it.
107024.m: The ulnar artery runs next to the ulna on the little-finger side.

107025.q: On which side of the wrist do you usually feel for the pulse?
a: On the back of the hand
In the middle of the palm
107025.e: On the thumb side of the wrist, the radial artery runs just under the skin. There the pulse can easily be felt with two fingers.
107025.m: You feel the pulse at the wrist on the thumb side.

107026.q: How does blood pressure change the further the blood gets from the heart?
a: It stays exactly the same everywhere
107026.e: The heart creates the pressure, and some of it is constantly lost through friction in the ever finer vessels. In the veins, the pressure is finally very low.
107026.m: The further from the heart, the lower the blood pressure.

107027.e: The pulmonary artery takes oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. It is still an artery, because it carries blood away from the heart.
107027.m: The pulmonary artery is an artery with oxygen-poor blood.

107028.q: Why do arteries have thicker walls than veins?
a: The blood pressure in them is higher
They lie right under the skin
107028.e: The heart pumps the blood into the arteries at high pressure. Their thick, muscular walls withstand this pressure.
107028.m: Arteries have thick walls because of the high pressure.

107029.q: What are the smallest branches of the arteries called?
107029.e: Arterioles are tiny arteries that lead the blood into the hair vessels. By getting narrower or wider, they control the blood supply.
107029.m: The smallest arteries are called arterioles.

107030.q: Which painless examination is used to check the carotid artery for narrowing?
107030.e: With an ultrasound device, the carotid artery can be viewed from outside and the blood flow measured. This shows narrowing without any operation.
107030.m: Narrowing of the carotid artery is found with ultrasound.

107031.q: How many common carotid arteries does a person have?
107031.e: There is a left and a right common carotid artery. Each supplies its own side of the head and neck.
107031.m: People have one carotid artery on the left and one on the right.

107032.q: Where can you feel the pulse well on the neck?
a: At the side of the neck, on the carotid artery
At the back of the neck, on the spine
At the front, on the voice box
Under the chin, on the bone
107032.e: The carotid artery lies at the side of the neck just under the skin. If you put two fingers there, you feel the blood throbbing with every heartbeat.
107032.m: At the side of the neck you can feel the pulse of the carotid artery.

107033.q: Into which two branches does the common carotid artery split?
107033.e: At about the level of the voice box, the common carotid artery forks. This forms the internal and the external carotid artery.
107033.m: The common carotid artery forks into an inner and an outer branch.

107034.q: Which organ does the internal carotid artery mainly supply?
107034.e: The internal carotid artery passes through the base of the skull into the inside of the head. There it supplies large parts of the brain and the eye with blood.
107034.m: The internal carotid artery brings blood to the brain.

107035.q: What does the external carotid artery supply?
107035.e: The external carotid artery stays outside the skull. Its branches supply the face, tongue, scalp and neck, among other parts.
107035.m: The external carotid artery supplies the face and neck.

107036.q: From which organ does the blood that flows through the carotid artery come?
107036.e: The heart pumps the blood into the aorta. The carotid arteries branch off from it and take the blood to the head.
107036.m: The carotid artery takes blood from the heart to the head.

107037.q: What do sensory cells at the fork of the carotid artery measure?
107037.e: The carotid sinus with its pressure sensors sits at the fork. They report the blood pressure to the brain so that it can control it.
107037.m: Sensors on the carotid artery measure blood pressure.

107038.q: To which organ does the portal vein take the blood?
107038.e: The portal vein collects blood from the stomach and intestines and takes it to the liver first. Only after that does it flow on to the heart.
107038.m: The portal vein leads to the liver.

107039.q: From which organs does the portal vein collect blood?
a: From the stomach, intestines and spleen
107039.e: Veins from the stomach, intestines, spleen and pancreas flow into the portal vein. In this way their blood reaches the liver first.
107039.m: The portal vein collects the blood of the digestive organs.

107040.q: After a meal, what does the blood in the portal vein contain in especially large amounts?
107040.e: The intestines absorb nutrients such as sugar and amino acids into the blood. Through the portal vein they reach the liver first, which processes them.
107040.m: After eating, the portal vein carries lots of nutrients.

107041.q: What is special about the portal vein?
a: It is a vein that leads into an organ instead of to the heart
It is an artery with no wall at all
It pumps the blood itself like a heart
It carries air instead of blood
107041.e: Normal veins take the blood back to the heart. The portal vein, by contrast, connects the network of capillaries in the intestines with a second network of capillaries in the liver.
107041.m: The portal vein is a vein between two networks of capillaries.

107042.q: What kind of blood flows in the portal vein?
a: Oxygen-poor blood from the digestive organs
107042.e: The portal vein is a vein. It carries blood from the stomach, intestines and spleen that has already given up oxygen but contains lots of nutrients.
107042.m: The portal vein carries blood from the digestive organs.

107043.q: Where does the portal vein get its name from?
a: It leads into the liver as if through a gate
It lies just behind the mouth
A researcher called Portal discovered it
It is as wide as a door
107043.e: The Latin word porta means gate. The portal vein enters the liver at a kind of entrance gate.
107043.m: The portal vein is the gate to the liver.

107044.q: What does the liver do with many substances from the portal vein blood?
a: It processes them and removes poisons
107044.e: The liver stores nutrients, converts them and makes poisonous substances harmless. That is why it makes sense for the blood from the intestines to flow through the liver first.
107044.m: The liver cleans and processes the blood from the portal vein.

107045.q: Which liver disease often leads to high pressure in the portal vein?
107045.e: In cirrhosis of the liver, the liver tissue becomes scarred and hard. The blood then backs up in the portal vein in front of the liver.
107045.m: A scarred liver can cause a blockage in the portal vein.

107046.q: Why should you measure on several days if high blood pressure is suspected?
a: Because blood pressure goes up and down during the day
Because you may only measure on Sundays
Because one measurement is always wrong
107046.e: Blood pressure changes with movement, stress, time of day and sleep. Only several measurements give a reliable picture.
107046.m: A single blood pressure reading says little; only many readings show the picture.

107047.q: What does the upper blood pressure reading show?
a: The pressure when the heart contracts
The pressure in the lungs when breathing in
The number of heartbeats per minute
The amount of blood in the body
107047.e: The upper reading is called the systolic blood pressure. It is produced when the ventricles contract and push blood into the arteries.
107047.m: The upper blood pressure reading is the pressure during a heartbeat.

107048.q: What does the lower blood pressure reading show?
a: The pressure when the heart relaxes
The pressure when the heart contracts
The number of heartbeats per minute
The amount of blood in the body
107048.e: Between two beats, the heart relaxes and fills with blood. The pressure in the arteries then drops to the lower reading.
107048.m: The lower blood pressure reading is the pressure while the heart rests.

107049.q: What is used to measure blood pressure on the upper arm?
107049.e: The cuff is put round the upper arm and pumped up. As it is slowly let down, the device measures the blood pressure.
107049.m: Blood pressure is measured with an arm cuff.

107050.q: What is the measurement called in which a portable device measures blood pressure regularly for a whole day?
107050.e: For 24-hour blood pressure monitoring, you wear a cuff with a small device for 24 hours. It also measures automatically during the night.
107050.m: 24-hour blood pressure monitoring records blood pressure over a whole day.

107051.q: Which instrument does the doctor use to hear the sounds in the arm when measuring blood pressure?
107051.e: The stethoscope is placed in the crook of the arm under the cuff. In this way you can hear the blood knocking and read off the blood pressure.
107051.m: A stethoscope lets you hear sounds inside the body.

107052.q: What is meant by “white coat hypertension”?
a: Blood pressure is only raised at the doctor’s because of nerves
Blood pressure rises when you wear white clothes
Blood pressure is always raised in winter
Blood pressure is only measured by doctors
107052.e: Some people are nervous at the doctor’s surgery, and their blood pressure rises there. At home their readings are then normal.
107052.m: Nerves at the doctor’s can raise the measured blood pressure.

107053.q: At what height should the cuff be when measuring blood pressure?
a: At the level of the feet
107053.e: If the cuff is higher or lower than the heart, the reading is wrong. That is why the arm should be placed so that the cuff is at heart level.
107053.m: When measuring blood pressure, the cuff belongs at heart level.

107054.q: When slowly letting the air out of the cuff, when do you hear the first tapping sounds?
a: When the cuff pressure falls below the upper value
As soon as the cuff is put on
Only when the cuff is completely empty
107054.e: As long as the cuff squeezes the artery shut, no blood flows and it is silent. When the pressure falls below the systolic value, blood forces its way through in spurts and you hear tapping.
107054.m: The first tapping when releasing the cuff shows the upper blood pressure value.

107055.q: Which mineral, found in large amounts in vegetables and fruit, can help to lower blood pressure?
107055.e: Potassium helps the body get rid of sodium through the kidneys and relaxes the blood vessels. Vegetables, fruit and pulses contain lots of it.
107055.m: A diet rich in potassium with plenty of vegetables is good for blood pressure.

107056.q: Which feature of the body clearly increases the risk of high blood pressure?
107056.e: When someone is very overweight, the heart has to work harder and the blood vessels are under more strain. Even losing some weight can lower blood pressure.
107056.m: Being very overweight strains the heart and blood pressure.

107057.q: Why do many people not notice their high blood pressure for a long time?
a: It often causes no symptoms for a long time
It turns the skin blue straight away
107057.e: High blood pressure usually does not hurt and causes no symptoms for a long time. That is why it is often only discovered when it is measured.
107057.m: You often cannot feel high blood pressure, so you should have it measured.

107058.q: Which seasoning can raise blood pressure if you eat a lot of it?
107058.e: Lots of table salt holds water in the body and can make blood pressure rise in many people. Ready meals often contain lots of hidden salt.
107058.m: Too much salt can push blood pressure up.

107059.q: Which brain condition becomes more likely after years of high blood pressure?
107059.e: Over time, high pressure damages the walls of the blood vessels. This increases the risk that a vessel in the brain becomes blocked or bursts.
107059.m: Untreated high blood pressure increases the risk of a stroke.

107060.q: What helps most to prevent high blood pressure?
107060.e: Regular exercise strengthens the heart and blood vessels and helps keep a healthy weight. Both lower the risk of high blood pressure.
107060.m: Regular exercise protects your blood vessels.

107061.q: What is the opposite of high blood pressure, meaning blood pressure that is too low, called?
107061.e: The prefix “hypo” means under or too little. That is why blood pressure that is low all the time is called hypotension.
107061.m: Blood pressure that is too low is called hypotension.

107062.q: Which organs that filter the blood can high blood pressure damage?
107062.e: The kidneys contain many fine vessels that filter the blood. Constant high pressure can damage these vessels and make the kidneys work less well.
107062.m: High blood pressure can damage the kidneys.

107063.q: Which drink raises blood pressure if you regularly drink a lot of it?
107063.e: Regularly drinking a lot of alcohol is one of the known causes of high blood pressure. Drinking less alcohol can lower blood pressure again.
107063.m: Lots of alcohol can raise blood pressure for good.

107064.q: What is the technical term for a short faint?
107064.e: A syncope is a short loss of consciousness from which you quickly recover. The term comes from Greek.
107064.m: A short faint is called a syncope.

a: The brain briefly gets too little blood
107065.e: In a faint, the brain briefly gets too little blood. As a result it lacks oxygen and you lose consciousness for a short time.
107065.m: In a faint, the brain briefly gets too little blood.

107066.q: How do you help a person who has briefly fainted and is breathing normally?
a: Lay them flat and raise their legs
Stand them up at once and make them walk
Give them cold water to drink
107066.e: If the legs are raised, more blood flows to the heart and brain. The person then usually comes round quickly.
107066.m: When someone faints, raise their legs.

107067.q: How long does an ordinary faint usually last?
a: Only seconds to a few minutes
107067.e: With a syncope, you quickly come round by yourself, usually after seconds. If the unconsciousness lasts longer, medical help is needed.
107067.m: An ordinary faint is over after a short time.

107068.q: Which situation can trigger a faint especially easily?
a: Standing for a long time in great heat
107068.e: When you stand for a long time in the heat, the blood vessels widen and blood collects in the legs. The brain then lacks blood.
107068.m: Standing for a long time in the heat can lead to fainting.

107069.q: Which warning sign often comes before a faint?
a: Everything goes black before your eyes
107069.e: Before a faint, dizziness, blackouts in your vision and nausea often occur. If you notice this, it is best to sit or lie down straight away.
107069.m: If everything goes black before your eyes, sit down straight away.

107070.q: A person stays unconscious but is breathing normally. How do you position them?
a: On their front with the face down
107070.e: In the recovery position, the airways stay clear and vomit can drain away. Then you call for help and keep checking the breathing.
107070.m: Unconscious people who breathe normally go into the recovery position.

107071.q: Why do some people briefly faint at the sight of blood?
a: A nerve reaction suddenly lowers pulse and blood pressure
The blood evaporates and makes you tired
The eyes are dazzled by the red
The stomach pulls all the blood towards it
107071.e: In this so-called vasovagal syncope, the nervous system overreacts. Heartbeat and blood pressure drop briefly, and the brain gets too little blood.
107071.m: A fright or the sight of blood can trigger a faint through the nerves.

107072.q: What happens in a circulatory collapse?
107072.e: In a circulatory collapse, blood pressure suddenly drops. The brain gets less blood, you feel weak and can collapse.
107072.m: A circulatory collapse is a sudden drop in blood pressure.

107073.q: Which movement makes some people dizzy because their blood pressure drops?
a: Getting up too quickly from lying down
Breathing out deeply while lying down
107073.e: When you get up quickly, blood flows into the legs before the circulation has adjusted. For a moment, the brain gets too little blood.
107073.m: If you get up quickly, your blood pressure can drop for a moment.

107074.q: When you stand still for a long time, where does a lot of blood pool?
107074.e: Because of gravity, blood collects in the veins of the legs. Without muscle movement, it only flows back to the heart slowly.
107074.m: When you stand for a long time, blood collects in the legs.

107075.q: What helps prevent a circulatory collapse on hot days?
a: Standing in the sun for a long time
107075.e: In the heat, the body loses a lot of fluid through sweating. If the blood is short of fluid, blood pressure drops more easily.
107075.m: Drinking enough in the heat protects your circulation.

107076.q: What helps against a circulatory collapse when standing for a long time?
a: Moving your toes and calves again and again
Holding your breath as long as possible
Holding your arms high above your head
107076.e: Working calf muscles squeeze the veins and push the blood towards the heart. This muscle pump keeps the circulation going.
107076.m: Moving calf muscles pump the blood back from the legs.

107077.q: What is a circulatory collapse caused by great heat called?
107077.e: In great heat, the blood vessels in the skin widen to give off warmth. This can make blood pressure drop so much that a heat collapse happens.
107077.m: Great heat can cause a heat collapse.

107078.q: What does the skin often look like during a circulatory collapse?
107078.e: In a collapse, the blood vessels in the skin narrow and a cold sweat breaks out. That is why the person looks pale.
107078.m: In a circulatory collapse, the skin is often pale and damp.

107079.q: What should you be careful about when getting up after a circulatory collapse?
a: Sit up slowly and only then stand up
Jump up at once and run
107079.e: The circulation needs time to recover. If you get up too quickly, you risk collapsing again.
107079.m: After a collapse, get up again only slowly.

a: Hardening and narrowing of the arteries
107080.e: In arteriosclerosis, substances build up in the artery wall. The artery becomes hard, narrow and less elastic.
107080.m: Arteriosclerosis makes the arteries hard and narrow.

107081.q: What is arteriosclerosis often called in everyday language?
107081.e: Because the deposits also contain lime (calcium), people often call it hardening of the arteries. The medical term is arteriosclerosis.
107081.m: In everyday language, arteriosclerosis is called hardening of the arteries.

107082.q: What are the deposits in the artery walls called?
107082.e: The deposits in the vessel wall are called plaques. They are made of fat, connective tissue and lime, among other things.
107082.m: The deposits in arteriosclerosis are called plaques.

107083.q: Which blood fat plays an important part in arteriosclerosis?
107083.e: Too much LDL cholesterol in the blood encourages plaques to form. That is why cholesterol levels are often measured at check-ups.
107083.m: Too much cholesterol in the blood encourages hardening of the arteries.

107084.q: Which habit is one of the strongest risk factors for arteriosclerosis?
107084.e: The substances in tobacco smoke damage the inner wall of the blood vessels. Deposits form more easily at the damaged spots.
107084.m: Smoking damages the blood vessels and encourages arteriosclerosis.

107085.q: What can happen if a coronary artery is blocked by arteriosclerosis?
107085.e: If a coronary artery is blocked, part of the heart muscle no longer gets any oxygen. This part dies if help does not come quickly.
107085.m: A blocked coronary artery causes a heart attack.

107086.q: What is the circulation problem in the legs called, in which people often have to stop and stand still?
107086.e: Narrowed leg arteries cause pain when walking that eases at rest. People with it often stop as if they were looking in shop windows, which is why it is also nicknamed “window-shopper’s disease”.
107086.m: Narrowed leg arteries cause intermittent claudication.

107087.q: How quickly does arteriosclerosis normally develop?
107087.e: The deposits grow slowly over years and decades. That is why a healthy lifestyle is worthwhile even when you are young.
107087.m: Arteriosclerosis develops gradually over many years.

a: A blood clot blocks a blood vessel
107088.e: In a thrombosis, a clot forms in a blood vessel. It can partly or completely block the vessel.
107088.m: In a thrombosis, a blood clot blocks a vessel.

107089.q: What is the blood clot that forms in a thrombosis called?
107089.e: The clot is called a thrombus. It is mainly made of blood platelets, fibrin and trapped blood cells.
107089.m: A blood clot in a vessel is called a thrombus.

107090.q: Where do thromboses form most often?
a: In the deep veins of the legs
In the tip of the nose
107090.e: In the deep veins of the legs, blood flows slowly against gravity. Clots form there most often.
107090.m: Thromboses usually form in the deep veins of the legs.

107091.q: Which dangerous consequence can a thrombosis in a leg vein have?
107091.e: If a clot comes loose, it can be carried with the blood through the heart into the lungs. There it blocks a vessel, which can be life-threatening.
107091.m: A clot that comes loose can cause a pulmonary embolism.

107092.q: Which situation increases the risk of a thrombosis?
a: Sitting for hours on a long-haul flight
107092.e: When you sit for a long time, the calf muscles hardly work and the blood flows slowly. That is why you should get up and move your legs on long journeys.
107092.m: Sitting for a long time without moving increases the risk of thrombosis.

107093.q: Which stockings are worn to prevent a thrombosis?
107093.e: Compression stockings put pressure on the legs. This makes the blood in the veins flow back to the heart faster.

107094.q: Which medicines are used to treat a thrombosis?
107094.e: Anticoagulants, often called blood thinners, stop the clot from growing. Then the body can slowly break it down.
107094.m: Anticoagulants stop a blood clot from growing.

107095.q: How can you often recognise a thrombosis in a leg vein?
a: The leg is swollen, warm and painful
The leg only itches on the sole
The leg feels ice cold and numb
107095.e: When blood backs up behind the clot, the leg swells. It often feels warm and tight and hurts.
107095.m: A swollen, warm and painful leg can be a sign of thrombosis.

a: A pale fluid in the lymph vessels
A hormone from the thyroid gland
107096.e: Lymph is a clear to yellowish fluid. It flows through the body in its own system of vessels.
107096.m: Lymph is a pale body fluid.

107097.e: A little fluid constantly leaks out of the capillaries into the tissue. Some of it is taken up by lymph vessels and is then called lymph.
107097.m: Lymph forms from the fluid between the cells.

107098.q: Where does lymph flow in the end?
a: Into the blood in the veins near the heart
107098.e: The large lymph ducts open into large veins near the heart. In this way the fluid returns to the bloodstream.
107098.m: Lymph flows back into the blood near the heart.

107099.q: What job do the lymph nodes have?
a: They filter the lymph and fight germs
They pump blood around the body
They store lime for the bones
107099.e: Lymph nodes are filter stations in the lymphatic system. Germs are caught there and fought by defence cells.
107099.m: Lymph nodes are filter stations of the body’s defences.

107100.q: Which white blood cells are found especially often in lymph?
107100.e: Lymphocytes are defence cells named after lymph. Erythrocytes are red blood cells and thrombocytes are blood platelets.
107100.m: Lymphocytes are defence cells that circulate in the lymph.

107101.q: What pushes lymph along the lymph vessels?
a: A lymph heart of its own in the chest
107101.e: The lymphatic system has no central pump like the heart. Muscle movements, breathing and valves in the lymph vessels push the lymph along.
107101.m: Muscle movements push lymph through the body.

107102.q: What is the largest lymph duct in the body called?
107102.e: The thoracic duct, in Latin ductus thoracicus, collects lymph from most of the body. It opens into the veins on the left side of the neck.
107102.m: The thoracic duct is the largest lymph duct.

107103.q: Why do the lymph nodes in the neck often swell when you have a sore throat?
a: Because they store water for the voice
107103.e: During an infection, defence cells multiply in the lymph nodes. This makes the nodes bigger and sometimes tender when pressed.
107103.m: Swollen lymph nodes show that the body is fighting germs.

107104.q: Which nutrients does lymph especially take up in the intestines?
107104.e: In the intestines, fats from food first pass into the lymph vessels. That is why the lymph there looks milky and cloudy.
107104.m: In the intestines, lymph mainly carries the fats taken up from food.

a: A build-up of water in the tissue
107105.e: With oedema, fluid collects in the tissue between the cells. The affected area swells up.
107105.m: Oedema is swelling caused by water in the tissue.

107106.q: Where does oedema appear especially often in many people?
a: On the ankles and lower legs
On the tip of the nose
107106.e: Because of gravity, fluid easily collects in the lower part of the legs. That is why the ankles often swell.
107106.m: Oedema often shows first on the ankles.

107107.q: How can you often recognise oedema on the skin?
a: Pressing with a finger leaves a dent
The skin glows in the dark
107107.e: If you press on the swollen area, the fluid is pushed away. The dent stays visible for a while.
107107.m: With oedema, a dent stays after pressing with a finger.

107108.q: Which heart condition often leads to oedema in the legs?
107108.e: If the heart pumps too weakly, the blood backs up in the veins. More fluid then leaks into the tissue of the legs.
107108.m: A weak heart can cause water to build up in the legs.

107109.q: Why is pulmonary oedema, water in the lungs, dangerous?
107109.e: In pulmonary oedema, fluid leaks into the air sacs of the lungs. Then there is no room for air, and the person struggles to breathe. It is an emergency.
107109.m: Pulmonary oedema is water in the lungs and a medical emergency.

107110.q: What is oedema called that is caused by lymph not draining properly?
107110.e: If lymph cannot drain properly, fluid builds up in the tissue. A special massage called lymphatic drainage can help.
107110.m: Blocked lymph drainage leads to lymphoedema.

107111.q: Why do feet often swell on hot summer days?
a: The vessels widen and fluid leaks out
The bones expand in the warmth
The muscles grow because of the heat
107111.e: Heat widens the blood vessels. As a result, more fluid leaks into the tissue, especially in the feet and ankles.
107111.m: Heat makes feet swell because the vessels widen.

107112.q: What are medicines that flush out oedema called?
107112.e: Water tablets, also called diuretics, make the kidneys get rid of more water and salt. This makes the build-up of water go down.
107112.m: Water tablets help the body get rid of stored water.

107113.q: Roughly what mass is the weight of the column of air resting on one square metre at sea level equal to?
107113.e: An air pressure of about 101,000 pascals means about 101,000 newtons per square metre. Divided by 9.81 N/kg, that gives about 10,300 kilograms, so roughly 10 tonnes.
107113.m: At sea level, a column of air of about 10 tonnes rests on every square metre.

107114.q: What is the SI unit of pressure?
107114.e: The unit of pressure is the pascal, named after Blaise Pascal. The newton is the unit of force, the joule of energy and the watt of power.

107115.q: Why does juice pour out of a can much better if you make a second hole in it?
a: Air can flow in through the second hole
The second hole makes the juice thinner
The hole makes the juice warmer
107115.e: Without a second hole, low pressure forms inside the can and the air pressure holds the juice back. When air can flow in, the pressure evens out and the juice flows smoothly.
107115.m: For liquid to pour out well, air must be able to flow in.

107116.q: Why are we not crushed by air pressure?
a: An equal counter-pressure exists inside the body
The skin does not let air through
Air pressure only acts on buildings
107116.e: Air and fluids in our body push outwards with an equal pressure. And because air pressure acts from all sides, the forces cancel out.
107116.m: The pressure in our body balances the air pressure.

107117.q: A full glass of water is covered with a postcard and turned upside down. Why does the water not fall out?
a: Air pressure pushes up against the card from below
The water sticks to the bottom of the glass
The card soaks up the water
The water becomes weightless in the glass
107117.e: Air pressure acts in all directions, including upwards. It presses the card against the glass more strongly than the weight of the water pulls it away.
107117.m: Air pressure also acts from below upwards.

107118.q: Why does a drink rise up a straw when you suck on it?
a: The outside air pressure pushes it up
The liquid becomes lighter than air
107118.e: When you suck, the pressure in your mouth gets smaller. The greater air pressure on the surface of the drink pushes the liquid up through the straw.
107118.m: When drinking through a straw, air pressure pushes the drink into your mouth.

107119.q: A match burns briefly inside a bottle, then a peeled hard-boiled egg is placed on the opening. Why does the egg slide in?
a: The air in the bottle cools, and air pressure pushes the egg in
The fire pulls the egg in magnetically
The heat makes the egg soft and runny
The bottle expands and gets wider
107119.e: The heated air in the bottle cools as soon as the egg seals the opening. The pressure inside drops, and the greater air pressure outside pushes the egg through the neck of the bottle.
107119.m: When the pressure in a bottle drops, the air pressure outside pushes the egg in.

107120.q: With what force does air at 100,000 Pa press on a palm with an area of 100 cm²?
107120.e: 100 cm² is 0.01 m². Force is pressure times area: 100,000 Pa · 0.01 m² = 1000 N.
107120.m: The force on a surface is calculated as pressure times area.

107121.q: What does the Greek word part “baros” in the word barometer mean?
107121.e: “Baros” means heaviness or weight in Greek, and “metron” means measure. So a barometer, in a way, measures the weight of the air.
107121.m: A barometer measures the weight of the air.

107122.q: What is a barometer called that continuously records air pressure on a strip of paper?
107122.e: In a barograph, air pressure moves a pen arm that draws on a rotating drum. This shows how the pressure changes over several days.
107122.m: A barograph records air pressure as a curve.

107123.q: What do many smartphones use a built-in air pressure sensor for?
a: To detect changes in height, such as floors
107123.e: Air pressure changes measurably even when you climb stairs. A pressure sensor can therefore tell whether you have gone up or down.
107123.m: An air pressure sensor in a mobile phone detects how high you have climbed.

107124.q: What happens to the almost airless metal capsule in an aneroid barometer when the air pressure rises?
107124.e: The capsule is almost empty and supported by a spring. When the air pressure rises, it is pressed in slightly, and a lever passes the movement on to the pointer.
107124.m: In an aneroid barometer, air pressure moves the capsule and with it the pointer.

107125.q: Why can a barometer measure air pressure even in a closed room?
a: Because the pressure inside and outside evens out
Because it measures through the wall
Because it only works with the window open
Because indoor air has no pressure
107125.e: Buildings are not airtight. Through small gaps, the air pressure in the room evens out with the pressure outside.
107125.m: In a normal room, the air pressure is the same as outside.

107126.q: Which label is written on many dial barometers at the lowest air pressure?
107126.e: Very low air pressure occurs in strong low-pressure areas, which often bring a lot of wind. That is why it often says “Stormy” there, while high pressure is marked “Fair”.
107126.m: Dial barometers often show the word stormy at very low pressure.

107127.q: The water rises in the spout of a weather glass (Goethe barometer). What does this show?
107127.e: Air is trapped in the closed body of the glass. When the air pressure outside falls, this air pushes the water up the open spout.
107127.m: If the water in the weather glass rises, the air pressure outside is falling.

107128.q: Why is the air pressure of all places converted to sea level for weather maps?
a: So that places at different heights can be compared
Because barometers only work by the sea
Because there is no air pressure in the mountains
So that the numbers get smaller
107128.e: Air pressure is always lower at altitude. If all values are converted to sea level, you can see the real high and low-pressure areas.
107128.m: For weather maps, air pressure is converted to sea level.

107129.q: In the famous experiment, what was inside the joined Magdeburg hemispheres?
107129.e: The air between the two hemispheres was pumped out. Inside there was therefore almost a vacuum.
107129.m: The Magdeburg hemispheres were almost airless inside.

107130.q: Why could the airless Magdeburg hemispheres hardly be pulled apart?
a: The air pressure outside pressed them together
A rubber band held them together
107130.e: Inside, there was no air pushing back. The air pressure outside pressed the hemispheres together with great force.
107130.m: The outside air pressure held the hemispheres together.

107131.q: How could the Magdeburg hemispheres be separated very easily after the experiment?
a: A valve was opened to let air in
They were hit with a hammer
They were twisted against each other
107131.e: As soon as air flowed in through the valve, the pressure inside and outside was the same. Then the hemispheres fell apart on their own.
107131.m: With air inside, the hemispheres simply fall apart.

107132.q: In the well-known picture of the experiment, how many horses pulled on the Magdeburg hemispheres?
107132.e: Guericke’s book shows two teams of 8 horses each pulling in opposite directions. Even so, they could hardly separate the spheres.
107132.m: Even 16 horses could hardly separate the airless hemispheres.

107133.q: One hemisphere is tied to a tree instead of a second team of horses. What changes?
a: Nothing, the tree pulls back with the same force
The spheres come apart at once
You need twice as many horses
107133.e: According to the principle of action and reaction, the tree provides the same counterforce as the second team. So half of the horses were actually unnecessary.
107133.m: A firm tree fully replaces the second team of horses.

107134.q: What was the Magdeburg hemispheres experiment meant to show?
a: How great the force of air pressure is
107134.e: The experiment showed that air presses on everything with great force. You only notice this when there is no air on one side.
107134.m: The Magdeburg hemispheres show the force of air pressure.

107135.q: Which device did Otto von Guericke need to remove the air from the hemispheres?
107135.e: Guericke built one of the first air pumps. With it, he sucked the air out of the joined hemispheres.
107135.m: Guericke pumped the air out with an air pump.

107136.q: How does the pulling force needed change if larger airless hemispheres are used?
107136.e: Force is pressure times area. Larger hemispheres give the air pressure more area to act on, so they are pressed together more strongly.
107136.m: The bigger the hemispheres, the more strongly the air presses them together.

107137.q: What would change if the hemisphere experiment were repeated on a high mountain?
a: The hemispheres would be a little easier to separate
The hemispheres could not be separated at all
The hemispheres would fall apart on their own
Nothing at all, air pressure is the same everywhere
107137.e: On a mountain, the air pressure is lower than in the valley. So the air presses the airless hemispheres together with less force.
107137.m: On the mountain, the lower air pressure presses the hemispheres together less strongly.

107138.q: What office did Otto von Guericke hold in Magdeburg?
107138.e: Otto von Guericke was mayor of Magdeburg for many years. Alongside his office, he did research as a natural scientist.
107138.m: Otto von Guericke was both a mayor and a researcher.

107139.q: Which device did Otto von Guericke invent around 1650?
107139.e: Guericke developed a pump that could suck air out of containers. With it, he was able for the first time to deliberately create an almost airless space.
107139.m: Otto von Guericke invented the air pump.

107140.q: In which century did Otto von Guericke live?
107140.e: Otto von Guericke was born in Magdeburg in 1602 and died in Hamburg in 1686. So he lived in the 17th century.
107140.m: Otto von Guericke lived from 1602 to 1686.

107141.q: Which war destroyed Guericke’s home town of Magdeburg in 1631?
107141.e: In 1631, Magdeburg was captured and almost completely destroyed in the Thirty Years’ War. Guericke survived and later helped to rebuild it.
107141.m: Magdeburg was destroyed in 1631 in the Thirty Years’ War.

107142.q: What did Otto von Guericke produce when he rubbed a spinning sphere with his hand?
107142.e: Rubbing gave the sphere an electric charge. Guericke’s device is considered one of the first electrostatic machines.
107142.m: Guericke’s sphere was one of the first electrostatic machines.

107143.q: In which language did Otto von Guericke write his main work about empty space?
107143.e: His main work was published in 1672 as “Experimenta Nova Magdeburgica”. At that time, Latin was the common language of scholars in Europe.
107143.m: In the 17th century, scholars often wrote in Latin.

107144.q: Which university is named after Otto von Guericke today?
107144.e: The Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg is named after the famous mayor and researcher.
107144.m: The university in Magdeburg honours Otto von Guericke with its name.

107145.q: Which old belief did Guericke disprove with his experiments?
a: That the Earth is a sphere
107145.e: Since Aristotle, many people believed that nature does not allow empty space. With his pump, Guericke showed that an almost airless space can be created.
107145.m: Guericke proved that an airless space is possible.

107146.q: In physics, what is meant by a vacuum?
a: A space without air and almost without particles
A space full of water vapour
A space with especially dense air
107146.e: A vacuum is a space from which air and other particles have largely been removed. The word comes from the Latin “vacuus”, meaning empty.
107146.m: A vacuum is an almost empty space without air.

107147.q: A ringing bell is placed under a glass bell jar, and the air is pumped out. What do you hear?
a: The ringing gets quieter and quieter
The ringing gets louder and louder
107147.e: Sound needs a medium such as air to travel. The less air there is in the jar, the less sound gets out.
107147.m: Sound cannot travel in a vacuum.

107148.q: Why does a vacuum flask keep drinks warm for a long time?
a: There is a vacuum between its walls
107148.e: The double wall of a vacuum flask is almost airless inside. Without air, hardly any heat is carried outwards by conduction or convection.
107148.m: The vacuum in the flask slows down heat loss.

107149.q: Why does vacuum-packed food stay fresh for longer?
a: Because hardly any oxygen reaches the food
Because it makes the food heavier
107149.e: Many germs and spoiling processes need oxygen. If the air is sucked out, the food spoils more slowly.
107149.m: Without air in the packaging, food spoils more slowly.

107150.q: Why does a vacuum cleaner suck up dust?
a: It creates low pressure, and air flows in
107150.e: A fan moves air out of the machine, so the pressure inside drops. The outside air pressure then pushes air and dust into the nozzle.
107150.m: A vacuum cleaner works with low pressure.

107151.q: Why is the glass bulb of a classic light bulb airless or filled with a protective gas?
a: So that the filament does not burn up
So that the bulb is lighter
So that the light is coloured
So that the bulb does not get warm
107151.e: The filament gets very hot. With oxygen from the air, it would quickly burn up, which is why the bulb contains no air.
107151.m: Without oxygen, the hot filament cannot burn up.

107152.q: A slightly inflated, knotted balloon lies under a glass bell jar. What happens when the air is pumped out of the jar?
a: The balloon stays the same size
107152.e: The air in the balloon pushes outwards, and the air in the jar pushes back. If the jar is pumped empty, there is nothing pushing back, and the trapped air expands the balloon.
107152.m: When the pressure around a balloon drops, the air inside it expands.

107153.q: Can a completely empty vacuum be created on Earth?
a: No, a few particles always remain
107153.e: Even the best vacuum pumps cannot remove all particles. That is why people speak of rough, fine or ultra-high vacuum, depending on how few particles remain.
107153.m: A perfect vacuum cannot be created.

107154.q: How does the Sun’s heat reach the Earth through almost empty space?
107154.e: Conduction and convection need particles, which are almost absent in space. Radiation, on the other hand, also travels through a vacuum.
107154.m: Heat radiation can even cross a vacuum.

107155.q: Why does a suction cup stick to a smooth tile?
a: The outside air pressure presses it on
It is coated with glue inside
107155.e: When you press it on, air is squeezed out from under the suction cup. The pressure underneath is then lower, and the outside air pressure presses it firmly on.
107155.m: A suction cup is pressed against the wall by air pressure.

107156.q: On which surface does a suction cup hold badly?
107156.e: A rough surface has tiny gaps through which air flows under the suction cup. Then the pressure evens out and it falls off.
107156.m: On rough surfaces, air gets under the suction cup.

107157.q: Why does a suction cup often hold better if you moisten it slightly first?
107157.e: A thin film of water fills tiny bumps at the edge. This means less air can get under the suction cup.
107157.m: A damp edge seals the suction cup better.

107158.q: Would a suction cup stick to a space station in airless space?
a: No, it does not hold without air pressure
Only if it is very cold
107158.e: A suction cup only works because air pressure pushes from outside. In a vacuum, this pressure is missing, so it does not hold.
107158.m: Without air pressure, no suction cup can stick.

107159.q: Which sea creature has many suckers on its arms?
107159.e: Octopuses have numerous suckers on their eight arms. They use them to cling to rocks and grab their prey.
107159.m: Octopuses hold on with many suckers.

107160.q: Why does a large suction cup hold more strongly than a small one?
a: The air pressure acts on a larger area
Large suction cups are more magnetic
107160.e: The holding force is the pressure difference times the area. With the same pressure difference, a larger area gives a larger force.
107160.m: The larger the area of the suction cup, the more strongly it holds.

107161.q: There is a vacuum under a suction cup with an area of 10 cm², and 100,000 Pa outside. What is the greatest force pressing it on?
107161.e: 10 cm² is 0.001 m². The force is 100,000 Pa · 0.001 m² = 100 N.
107161.m: The holding force of a suction cup is the pressure difference times the area.

107162.q: What do glaziers often use to carry large panes of glass?
107162.e: Suction lifters have one or more large suction cups with a handle. They hold securely on the smooth glass without scratching it.
107162.m: Glaziers carry panes with suction lifters.

107163.q: Why does a suction cup come off when you pull its small tab?
a: Air flows under the suction cup
107163.e: The tab lifts the edge so that air flows under the suction cup. The pressure evens out and nothing presses it on any more.
107163.m: If you let air under the suction cup, it comes off.

107164.q: You hold a tube filled with water closed at the top with your finger. Why does the water stay in it?
a: Air pressure from below holds it
The finger sucks the water up
The water freezes in the tube
The water sticks to the finger
107164.e: No air can flow in at the top. If a little water runs out, the pressure at the top drops, and the outside air pressure from below holds the water back.
107164.m: A pipette closed at the top holds the liquid by air pressure.

107165.q: Why does the liquid run out of the pipette as soon as you take your finger off the top?
a: Air flows in at the top and evens out the pressure
The finger has warmed the liquid
107165.e: With the end open, the air pressure is the same at the top and bottom. Then gravity pulls the liquid down and out.
107165.m: With its end open, a pipette runs empty.

107166.q: Why does liquid rise into a dropper when you let go of the squeezed rubber bulb?
a: The outside air pressure pushes it in
The liquid gets warm and rises
107166.e: Squeezing pushes air out. The bulb then expands again, the pressure inside drops, and air pressure pushes the liquid in.
107166.m: Air pressure pushes the liquid into the dropper.

107167.q: What is a volumetric pipette used for in the laboratory?
a: To measure exactly one fixed volume
107167.e: A volumetric pipette has only one mark and measures exactly one particular volume, for example 10 ml. A graduated pipette, on the other hand, has a scale for different amounts.
107167.m: A volumetric pipette measures exactly one fixed volume.

107168.q: A winemaker takes wine out of a barrel with a long glass tube. How does the wine stay in the tube as it is pulled out?
a: He keeps the top of the tube closed with his thumb
107168.e: When the tube is closed at the top, air pressure from below holds the wine in the tube. When the winemaker takes his thumb away, the wine flows into the glass.
107168.m: A glass tube for barrels works like a large pipette.

107169.q: Which amounts are typically measured with a micropipette in the laboratory?
a: A few microlitres to about one millilitre
107169.e: Micropipettes are made for very small amounts of liquid. A microlitre is a thousandth of a millilitre.
107169.m: Micropipettes are used to measure tiny amounts of liquid.

107170.q: Where do you read the level of water in a pipette?
a: At the bottom of the curve, at eye level
At the top edge of the glass wall
From above at an angle with one eye
107170.e: In a narrow tube, water forms a surface that curves downwards, the meniscus. You read it at its lowest point at eye level.
107170.m: With water, you read at the bottom of the meniscus.

107171.q: Why should you never suck liquids into a pipette with your mouth in the laboratory?
a: The mouth is too weak for it
107171.e: In the laboratory, people often work with poisonous or corrosive substances. That is why you always use a rubber bulb or a pipette filler.
107171.m: Fill pipettes only with a bulb or a pipette filler, never with your mouth.

107172.q: You are standing still, but the air pressure drops because of a low. What does a barometric altimeter show?
a: No value at all any more
107172.e: Such an altimeter calculates height from air pressure. If the pressure falls because of the weather, it wrongly takes this as a climb and has to be reset.
107172.m: Changes in the weather can fool a barometric altimeter.

107173.q: A half-empty plastic bottle is closed on a summit and carried down to the valley. What happens?
107173.e: Air at the low pressure of the summit is trapped in the bottle. In the valley, the outside air pressure is greater and squashes the bottle.
107173.m: In the valley, the higher air pressure squashes a bottle closed at the top.

107174.q: What helps when your ears feel pressure in a fast cable car?
a: Holding your breath for a long time
107174.e: When you swallow or yawn, the Eustachian tube opens briefly. This evens out the pressure in the middle ear with the outside air pressure.
107174.m: Swallowing helps to even out the pressure in your ears.

107175.q: How great is the air pressure on a 3500-metre Alpine summit compared with the sea?
107175.e: Air pressure decreases with height. At about 3500 metres, it is only about two thirds as great as at sea level.
107175.m: On high Alpine summits, the air pressure is only about two thirds of that at sea level.

107176.q: Roughly how great is the air pressure on the summit of Mount Everest compared with sea level?
107176.e: At almost 8850 metres, the air pressure is around 300 to 340 hPa. That is about one third of the pressure at sea level.
107176.m: On Mount Everest, the air pressure is only about one third of that at sea level.

107177.q: Why is the cabin of an airliner pressurised at high altitude?
a: Because the air outside is too thin to breathe
So that the plane flies faster
So that the cabin gets warmer
So that the engines are quieter
107177.e: At around 10 kilometres, the air pressure is very low. Without a pressurised cabin, the passengers would get too little oxygen.
107177.m: The pressurised cabin protects passengers from the thin air at altitude.

107178.q: Why does a weather balloon burst at high altitude?
a: The outside air pressure falls, and it expands
107178.e: The higher it goes, the less air presses from outside. The gas in the balloon expands until the skin tears.
107178.m: A weather balloon gets bigger and bigger at altitude until it bursts.

107179.q: Why do many endurance athletes sometimes train at altitude, for example in St. Moritz?
a: In thin air the body makes more red blood cells
The air at altitude contains more oxygen
Muscles only grow in the cold
107179.e: At lower air pressure, less oxygen gets into the blood with each breath. The body adapts by making more red blood cells.
107179.m: Altitude training stimulates the production of red blood cells.

107180.q: Which letter marks a high-pressure area on German-language weather maps?
107180.e: On German-language weather maps, H stands for “Hoch” (high) and T for “Tief” (low). The letters mark the centre of the pressure area.
107180.m: An H on a German weather map shows a high.

107181.q: What is the wind usually like at the centre of a high?
107181.e: At the centre of a high, the air pressure changes only a little over a long distance. That is why there is usually only a light wind there.
107181.m: At the centre of a high, there is usually little wind.

107182.q: What can a long-lasting high bring in summer?
107182.e: A stable summer high brings lots of sunshine and hardly any rain. If it lasts a long time, it can become very hot and dry.
107182.m: A long summer high can bring heat and drought.

107183.q: What are highs and lows given in weather reports in Central Europe?
107183.e: Highs and lows are given first names, for example High Paul or Low Anna. This makes them easier to tell apart.
107183.m: Highs and lows have first names.

107184.q: How do highs and lows take turns when they are named in Central Europe?
a: Female and male names swap every year
Highs are always named after cities
The names are drawn by lot and never swapped
107184.e: In the past, lows only got female names and highs only male names. Since 1998, this has swapped every year to make it fair.
107184.m: Highs and lows swap female and male names every year.

107185.q: Why are nights during a high often especially cold?
a: Without clouds, a lot of heat escapes into space
The high sucks up the heat
In a high, the Sun does not shine at night
107185.e: When the sky is clear, the ground gives off heat freely at night. Clouds would hold back some of this heat.
107185.m: Clear nights during a high are often especially cold.

107186.q: Why does fine dust pollution often rise in the Swiss Plateau during a winter high?
a: The air hardly mixes, and pollutants build up
A high produces fine dust itself
In a high, dust rains from the sky
The Sun turns fog into dust
107186.e: Under a high in winter, cold air is often trapped near the ground. Exhaust fumes from traffic and heating are then not carried away and build up.
107186.m: In stable high-pressure weather, pollutants build up in the air.

107187.q: Where does the bitter cold in Central Europe often come from in winter?
a: From a high over the Sahara
107187.e: In winter, a strong high often forms over cold Russia. It can steer very cold, dry continental air westwards as far as Central Europe.
107187.m: A Russian high can bring Central Europe severe winter cold.

107188.q: Which letter stands for a low on English-language weather maps?
107188.e: An area of low pressure is called a “low” in English, so an L is used. On German-language maps, a T is used instead.
107188.m: On English weather maps, L stands for a low.

107189.q: What is the technical term for an area of low pressure?
107189.e: In meteorology a low is called a cyclone, because the air circles around it. The counterpart for a high is the anticyclone.
107189.m: The technical term for a low is cyclone.

107190.q: Which warm downslope wind often blows in Swiss Alpine valleys when a low approaches from the west?
107190.e: An approaching low creates a pressure difference between the south and north sides of the Alps. The air flows over the Alps and descends into the valleys as the warm Föhn.
107190.m: A low in the west often triggers the Föhn in the Alps.

107191.q: Why is it often stormy in a strong low?
a: The air pressure changes a lot over a short distance
The air there is especially heavy
The Sun shines more strongly there
107191.e: The greater the pressure difference over a short distance, the faster the air flows. In strong lows, this difference is especially large.
107191.m: Large pressure differences over a short distance cause strong winds.

107192.q: What major damage did Hurricane Lothar mainly cause in Switzerland in 1999?
a: It blew down millions of trees
It made many lakes dry up
It brought a metre of snow to the Swiss Plateau
107192.e: On 26 December 1999, Storm Lothar swept across Switzerland with very strong gusts of wind. It snapped and uprooted millions of trees.
107192.m: In 1999, Storm Lothar blew down millions of trees in Switzerland.

107193.q: What is the air pressure like at the centre of a strong tropical cyclone?
a: Exactly the same as all around
107193.e: Tropical cyclones are especially powerful low-pressure areas. At their centre, the air pressure is much lower than in the surroundings, so the air rushes in with great force.
107193.m: At the centre of a tropical cyclone, the air pressure is very low.

107194.q: What is a low called that forms when the ground is strongly heated?
107194.e: When the ground is strongly heated, the warm air rises and the pressure at the ground falls. This is how a heat low often forms over Spain in summer, for example.
107194.m: A heat low forms over strongly heated ground.

107195.q: How does the barometer reading change at a place over which a low passes?
a: It falls first and then rises again
It rises first and then stays high
It stays the same the whole time
107195.e: As the low approaches, the air pressure falls until the centre has passed. After that, it rises again.
107195.m: When a low passes, the barometer falls and then rises again.

107196.q: What happens to the mercury column in the barometer when the air pressure rises?
107196.e: Air pressure presses on the mercury in the dish and holds up the column in the tube. The greater the air pressure, the higher the column.
107196.m: When the air pressure rises, the mercury column rises too.

107197.q: What is the almost empty space above the mercury column in Torricelli’s tube called?
107197.e: When the tube is turned upside down, the mercury sinks a little. Above it remains an almost empty space, the Torricellian vacuum.
107197.m: Above the mercury in the tube, the Torricellian vacuum forms.

107198.q: What stays the same if you hold Torricelli’s tube at an angle?
a: The vertical height of the mercury column
The length of the mercury column
The mass of the mercury in the tube
The size of the empty space
107198.e: Air pressure holds up a column of a particular vertical height. In a tilted tube, the mercury fills more of the tube’s length, but the height stays the same.
107198.m: In a barometer, only the vertical height of the column counts.

107199.q: How does the height of the mercury column depend on the diameter of the tube?
a: Not at all, it is the same for any width
The wider the tube, the higher
The narrower the tube, the lower
It is only the same for metal tubes
107199.e: The pressure of a column of liquid depends only on its height and density. That is why mercury rises to the same height in wide and narrow tubes.
107199.m: The height of the mercury column does not depend on the width of the tube.

107200.q: Which unit of pressure is named after Evangelista Torricelli?
107200.e: One torr is almost exactly equal to the pressure of a mercury column 1 millimetre high. The unit honours Torricelli.
107200.m: The pressure unit torr is named after Torricelli.

107201.q: Roughly how long was the glass tube in Torricelli’s experiment?
107201.e: The tube was about one metre long and closed at one end. It had to be longer than the mercury column that air pressure can hold up.
107201.m: Torricelli’s tube was about one metre long.

107202.q: Why are mercury barometers hardly used any more today?
a: Because mercury is solid at room temperature
107202.e: Mercury vapour is poisonous and harms people and the environment. That is why aneroid barometers and electronic sensors are used today.
107202.m: Because it is poisonous, mercury is avoided today.

107203.q: Roughly how many times denser than water is mercury?
107203.e: Mercury has a density of about 13.6 g/cm³, water about 1 g/cm³. That is why a mercury column is much shorter than a water column with the same pressure.
107203.m: Mercury is about 13.6 times as dense as water.

107204.q: What is meant by an implosion?
a: An object is crushed inwards by pressure from outside
107204.e: In an implosion, the pressure outside is much greater than inside. The casing gives way and collapses inwards, unlike in an explosion.
